title: Office Politics (Informal Power Structures)
description: The unofficial rules, alliances, and power plays that determine who gets ahead in a workplace, beyond the formal org chart. It’s how decisions are actually made: through influence, not just authority.
shortDescription: The unofficial rules, alliances, and power plays that determine who gets ahead in a workplace, beyond the formal org chart. It’s how decisions are actually made: through influence, not just authority.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: The unofficial rules, alliances, and power plays that determine who gets ahead in a workplace, beyond the formal org chart. It’s how decisions are actually made: through influence, not just authority.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: The person who controls the meeting agenda controls what gets discussed and what gets buried.
Information is shared selectively: who gets the heads‑up before the big announcement?
A coalition of three directors agrees privately before a board vote, making the official debate a formality.
“Key person dependencies” are weaponized: “You can’t fire me; I’m the only one who knows how this works.”

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Lunch meetings where real decisions are made, then rubber‑stamped in formal sessions.
People building relationships with the boss’s boss to bypass their direct manager.
Gossip as intelligence: who’s rising, who’s falling, who’s protected.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “It’s not what you know, it’s who you know.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: Formal processes (performance reviews, promotion boards) don’t match actual outcomes.
You’re always the last to know about changes that affect you.
Access to key people is blocked by gatekeepers.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Formal authority is only one source of power. Social psychologists French and Raven identified other bases: expert power, referent power, informational power. Office politics is the arena where these are traded and fought over.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Map the informal network: who talks to whom, who influences whom, who are the “shadow decision‑makers.”
Build genuine, not transactional, relationships across the organization.
Be useful: become a source of information or expertise that others need, so you have currency.
Avoid taking sides in wars unless absolutely necessary; neutrality can be a powerful position.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Pretending office politics doesn’t exist and refusing to engage. The game plays you whether you play or not.
Over‑politicking and becoming known as a schemer; trust evaporates quickly.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A new VP arrives with a mandate for change. She ignores the network of long‑tenured middle managers who control budgets and communication. Her initiatives are “agreed” in meetings but never executed. She complains that the organization is resistant. She failed to see that the real power wasn’t in the C‑suite but in the informal coalition she never bothered to meet.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: The org chart is the skeleton. Office politics is the nervous system. You can’t move the body by pulling on bones alone.
